bio.en: Shreyas Doshi is a product leader and one of today's most consistently insightful voices on the craft of product management, drawing on senior product roles at Google, Twitter, Yahoo, and Stripe; this is a live-recorded edition of his conversation.
bio.zh: Shreyas Doshi 是一位产品领导者，也是当下对产品管理手艺最具持续洞察力的声音之一，其经验来自在 Google、Twitter、Yahoo 和 Stripe 的高级产品职务；本期为其对话的现场录制版。

summary.en: Shreyas shares his philosophy of high-leverage product work, including the art of saying no, focusing on outcomes over output, and protecting cognitive bandwidth for the few things that matter. He discusses how to develop product taste, the discipline of ignoring most requests, and why great PMs think in terms of leverage and systems. The episode is a dense, actionable masterclass in the craft of product management.
summary.zh: Shreyas 分享了他关于高杠杆产品工作的理念，包括说“不”的艺术、聚焦产出之上的成果、以及为少数要事保护认知带宽。他讨论了如何培养产品品味、忽略大多数请求的自律，以及为什么优秀的产品经理以杠杆与系统的方式思考。本期是关于产品管理手艺的、信息密集且可落地的导师课。

turns.en: Right, so let's see, the first question is why am I so busy? Why am I so busy? And the background is that I have spent most of my career just being completely stressed out, just absolutely stressed out every day. And there were many reasons for it, but one of the core reasons was I was always super busy, and there was always work I felt like I couldn't do that I wanted to do, and so I would go home at the end of the day, and even if I had worked hard, I'd just feel dissatisfied. (06:27): And so that was a constant fixture of my life as a PM, PM leader, and it's only... So I did product work for about 20 years before I started this new chapter of my career. And I think I only fixed it in the last three or four years of my career as a PM leader. But that means that there were about 16 or 17 years where I was just incredibly busy, and because I was incredibly busy, I was extremely stressed, and even though I was doing a good job, I was not feeling very good inside. And then, that showed up in my body, like all sorts of pains and aches I realized were actually not physical pains and aches. They were pains and aches from the stress.
turns.zh: 好的，那我们来看看第一个问题：为什么我这么忙？为什么我这么忙？背景是，我职业生涯的大部分时间都处于极度压力之下，每天都压力重重。造成这种情况的原因有很多，但核心原因之一是我总是超级忙碌，总有做不完的工作，而我又想做更多的事。每天工作结束后，即便已经很努力了，但内心还是会感到不满足。（06:27）这就是我作为产品经理和PM领导者的日常生活常态。直到……我才开始改变。之前做了约20年的产品工作后，才开启了职业生涯的新篇章。我觉得自己是在过去三四年的PM领导生涯中才解决了这个问题。但这意味着有16、17年的时间我都异常忙碌。由于压力过大，我的工作质量受到了影响，内心也备受煎熬。这些情绪最终反映在身体上，比如各种疼痛和不适，起初我以为是身体问题，但后来发现这些都是压力带来的心理反应。

turns.en: Yeah, and so here's the thing, when we talk about being busy, and managing your time, energy, all of that, I mean, this is a group of senior product people, so you all know that. Take tips and techniques, like maintain a to-do list. I found the LNO framework very useful for me, which I've shared before. I used to like working out of a calendar, those types of things. And I think you're all familiar with those things, but what I wanted to call out is that, at some point in our product career, we reach something, we reach an immovable force that will just overwhelm us, no matter what we do. (08:39): And that force is a scope. Okay, so as we grow in our product career, our scope grows, and we kind of like that, which is all great, but at some point, if you haven't already gotten there, many of you have, but for those of you who haven't, you will get there, where your scope will be so large, that no matter what you do in terms of efficiency, whatever framework you use for prioritization, whatever framework or tool you use to manage your to-do list, whatever tools and techniques you use, whatever prioritization you do, your scope is so large that you are still going to be incredibly busy. (09:21): And so that's what I faced, like I was saying for the first about 16, 17 years of working on products, and only in the last 3 or 4 years was I able to kind of find some answers on how to deal with that scope. And so perhaps we can talk about that, what do you think?
turns.zh: 是啊，说到忙碌和时间管理、精力管理这些话题，我知道你们都是资深产品人，所以这些概念你们都很熟悉。可以借鉴一些技巧，比如保持待办清单。我之前分享过的LNO框架对我很有用。我过去常用日历来安排工作，这些方法大家都熟悉。但我想强调的是，在产品生涯的某个阶段，我们会遇到一个无法突破的阻力，无论怎么努力都无法摆脱它。（08:39）这个阻力就是范围过大了。随着产品生涯的成长，项目范围也会扩大，这本该是好事，但在某个阶段，如果你还没遇到这种情况（很多人已经经历过），但总有一天你会遇到：你的项目范围会大到无论你如何提高效率，无论用什么优先级框架，无论用什么工具来管理待办清单，无论如何排优先级，范围都太大了，你还是会忙得不可开交。（09:21）这就是我面临的挑战，正如我前面提到的，我在产品工作的16、17年里都是如此，直到最近三四年才找到应对这种范围过大的方法。或许我们可以聊聊这个，你们怎么看？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, so you're basically saying there's all these productivity tricks, ways to do more faster. And no matter how many of these tools you've got, you are just going to take on more and more work, and they'll peter out? I'll say many of my most popular newsletters posts are, "Here's productivity tricks and tips." And so people are always looking for these. And I'm curious to hear where you go with this, of just like that is not the answer long term, there's a different approach?
turns.zh: 是啊，所以你基本上是在说，有各种各样的提高效率的技巧，能让你更快地完成更多工作。然而无论你拥有多少这类工具，你最终还是会接下越来越多的工作，结果却逐渐力不从心？我得说，我最受欢迎的新闻通讯文章里有很多都是关于“提高效率的技巧和窍门”的。所以人们总是对这些内容感兴趣。我很想听听你对此的看法——难道这不是长远的解决之道吗？或许还有其他更有效的方法？

turns.speaker: Shreyas Doshi
turns.en: Yes, and so the challenge is the following. How many of you are going through some kind of annual planning right now or you're planning on going through annual planning? Please. Everybody loves annual planning, great. So let's take annual planning. If you are a high-level manager, leader within a company, what does your month look like? Or in some cases, unfortunately, what do your two or three months look like when you are going through annual planning? It's all these kind of spreadsheets to fill out, and meetings to have, and dependencies, and priorities, and stakeholders to meet, and so on. And so I noticed, for instance, that at some point, that was making me really busy, and then that was making me feel guilty now, because I had my team to look after and to support, and then I had product decisions to make and various other things, and I've gone on some planning retreat or whatever. (11:15): And there you go, you last four, five, six, weeks, does that sound familiar to folks? Yeah? Okay, so I noticed that I needed to change that at some point, and actually found a solution, again, late in my career, but I found a solution, because I asked myself this question, which is, "Why am I so busy? I'm doing all the efficiency things, I'm managing my to-do list like a champ. I have my calendar set up just right. I have my routine set up just right. I'm working out so that I'm engaged at work, I'm productive, I'm doing all of that. Why am I so busy? Oh, it's planning season, and that is supposed to take up four to six weeks." And this was at Stripe when I encountered this. So that is supposed to take up four to six weeks. (12:03): Well, I realized that you don't have to do that. And so at some point in my time at Stripe, what I realized is the following, we go through a whole all sorts of just rituals around planning for four to six weeks. Then, we emerge and we share our plan with our executives. You know the questions they're going to ask, like, "If money were no concern, what would you do? What is your ambitious plan? So if we gave you five more engineers, what would you do? What other things would you include in the roadmap?" Right? The standard stuff. And so you emerge, you do your presentation, and then you publish the plan, and then you start the new year with a lot of enthusiasm and a lot of excitement. And January goes fine, until you get three customer escalations for features that were not in your plan. And so now, you try to figure out how you're going to revise resources. (13:03): You go talk to some dependency team that's going to sort of support these new features from these customer escalations. And you go through that process, and you revise your plan again. And then, usually by the time it's last week of February, everybody's forgotten the actual plan. And now, we are executing off of some other list somewhere. And by the way, when you mention this at times, politely of course, you might mention like, "You know, I'm noticing we are not actually really using the plan that we spent four to six weeks minimum doing." And then, some smart person in the room chimes in with, "Plans are useless, but planning is everything." (13:52): I don't know, Eisenhower, somebody else, I don't know who said this, "Plans are useless, but planning is everything." Nobody knows what it means. Nobody knows what that means, but everybody appreciates, "Ah, plans are useless, but planning is everything." Right? So I went through a few years of this. And then I go, "You know what? I'm going to bend some rules here." And so what I realized, Lenny, is you don't have to go through these four to six weeks, and it was an accident. Basically, what happened is around that time, the product I was working on, Stripe Connect, it's like a major product for Stripe, major, major business for Stripe. And I had put together a product strategy, like a real product strategy for this product. (14:44): And so this must have been earlier in the year. And so now, planning season came along. And the interesting I found is that because I had a real product strategy, not one of those fake ones, a real product strategy that I had gotten alignment on with everybody, my planning for this major product for Stripe took me like three days. Right, so while a lot of my peers, unfortunately, for their own products, were in this four-to-six week cycle of planning, and meeting, and blah, blah, blah, I just put it all together in three days, and whatever artifacts were needed, I put them together. (15:27): I did not fill out some templates. That's where it's about bending the rules, because if a template doesn't make sense, why should I fill it out? There's no need to fill it out. And so that's when I realized that actually, if you have a real product strategy, a real one that everybody is aligned with, that you have got pre-alignment on, then a lot of this nonsense we tend to do with annual planning actually goes away. Now, you still have to do some resource allocation and all of that, but even there, you don't need that false precision. How many of you have gotten into arguments about, "So should it be eight engineers for this team in 2025, or nine engineers for this team in 2025?" (16:11): Like, who cares? We all know that even those numbers that we set up, we don't actually follow through on them, as 2025 happens. So that's just an example of where we spend a lot of time on things that we think are strategic, that we think are important, but actually, we ought to spend that time on other much higher leverage things. Right, now it does require some upfront work, in this case upfront work on a clear product strategy that everybody understands, that everybody's aligned on. But frankly, if you have that, planning should be a breeze.

是的，接下来要讨论的挑战是这样的：你们当中有多少人正在进行年度规划，或者正计划开展年度规划？请举手。大家都喜欢年度规划，这很棒。那么让我们先从年度规划说起。如果你是一家公司的管理层或高层领导，你每个月的日程安排是怎样的？或者在某些情况下，不幸的是，当你进行年度规划时，你的两到三个月时间又会被各种表格填写、会议、依赖关系、优先级排序以及与利益相关者沟通等事务占据。我注意到，比如说，这曾让我非常忙碌，后来又让我感到内疚，因为我既要照顾和支持团队，又要做产品决策，还参加各种规划研讨会等活动（11:15）。这最后四到五周的时间，听起来是不是很熟悉？是吧？好的，我意识到自己需要改变现状，实际上是在职业生涯的后期才找到解决方案，因为我问了自己一个问题："为什么我这么忙？我已经在做各种提高效率的事情了，我的待办清单管理得很好，日程安排也很合理，日常习惯也很到位，我还能保持工作投入和高效，但为什么还是这么忙？"哦，原来是因为规划季来了，而这通常要占用四到六周的时间。（12:03）后来我意识到其实没必要这样。在Stripe工作期间，我发现我们会用四到六周的时间进行各种规划仪式，然后向高管汇报。但你们都知道高管会问什么问题："如果资金不受限制，你会怎么做？你的宏伟计划是什么？如果再给你五名工程师，你会怎么做？路线图里还应该加入哪些内容？"等等标准问题。然后你汇报完毕，发布计划后，大家兴致勃勃地迎接新年。但一月份一切顺利，直到三月份客户紧急提出功能需求，而这些需求根本不在你的计划之内。于是你开始调整资源，找依赖团队支持这些新功能，重新修订计划。通常到二月底，大家就把原计划忘得一干二净，现在大家又在执行其他清单了。顺便说一句，当你礼貌地提到这一点时，可能会有人附和："计划是无用的，但规划才是最重要的。"（13:52）我不知道，艾森豪威尔还是其他人说过这句话，"计划是无用的，但规划才是最重要的。"没人明白这句话的深意。但大家都附和道："啊，是啊，计划是无用的，但规划才是最重要的。"对吧？所以我经历了这样的循环几年后，终于决定打破常规。于是我意识到，莱尼，
你们不必经历这四到六周的规划过程，这次规划完全是个意外。事情是这样的，当时我负责的Stripe Connect产品对Stripe来说是个重磅级项目，是公司的核心业务。我为这个产品制定了完整的产品战略，是一份真正意义上的产品战略，并且得到了所有团队成员的一致认可。（14:44）当时正值年度规划季，我发现因为我制定了切实可行的产品战略——而不是那种虚假的规划——所以我只用了三天时间就完成了Stripe这个重大产品的规划工作。与此同时，很多同事为了自己的产品不得不经历四到六周的规划周期，不断开会、讨论各种细节，而我只用了三天就整合好了所有要素，所需的文档也都是自己整理的。（15:27）我没有填写那些模板。这就是打破规则的例子——如果模板毫无意义，为什么还要强制填写呢？根本没必要。所以我意识到，如果你有真正意义上的产品战略，得到所有团队成员认可、预先达成共识的战略，那么很多年度规划中的无意义环节其实都可以省掉。当然，你还是需要进行资源分配等工作，但即便如此，也没必要追求虚假的精确性。你们中有多少人会为2025年这个团队需要8名工程师还是9名工程师这种问题争论不休？（16:11）谁在乎呢？我们都知道，即使设定了这些数字，到2025年时也根本不会按计划执行。这只是个例子，说明我们在很多自以为是战略性重要的事情上浪费了大量时间，但实际上这些时间本可以用在更高效的任务上。当然，这需要前期投入，比如制定一份清晰、全员理解、达成共识的产品战略。但说实话，只要有这样的基础，规划工作就能变得轻而易举。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what would be your kind of tactical tip for folks that want to do this better? I know there's probably a billion examples of these sorts of things you shared, so planning is an example. Folks that want to be less busy, maybe on that one is it give yourself very little time, and focus on strategy, and let that be the plan, basically, versus every single person and their roadmap for the next six months. What's the piece of advice you'd share there? And then, I want to move on to the next question, because I want to make sure we get through all these questions.
turns.zh: 那么，对于那些想把这件事做得更好的人，你有什么实用的策略建议呢？我知道你分享过无数类似的例子，所以规划就是其中一个例子。对于那些想减少忙碌的人来说，或许可以这样做：给自己留出极少的时间，专注于制定策略，让这份策略成为核心计划，而不是每个人都制定自己未来六个月的路线图。你能给出这方面的建议吗？接下来，我想转到下一个问题了，因为我要确保我们能把所有问题都讨论完。

turns.speaker: Shreyas Doshi
turns.en: Yes, there's definitely a specific tip, which is if you do have a strategy that will make a lot of your prioritization problems go away, it will make a lot of planning problems go away. And even if you do have some escalation from sales, which you will, or from support, or somewhere else, you now have at least a more rigorous framework to figure out what to do with that escalation. So there's definitely that. (17:48): But I think other thing I want to share is that, and this was my other realization as I asked the question, "Why am I so busy?" is I realized that I am so busy because I'm not making good product decisions. Okay, now, you have to understand, by this time I'm like 15 years into building products and whatever, 11 years into being a product manager. And so I think I'm pretty good. That's my kind of self-image. But then, again, if I'm being honest to myself, I'm not making as good product decisions as I can. So can I share an example of that?
turns.zh: 是的，确实有一个具体的建议，那就是如果你制定了一个策略，它能解决很多优先级排序的问题，也能解决很多规划方面的问题。即使你确实遇到了来自销售、支持部门或其他方面的紧急需求，你现在至少有了一个更严格的框架来处理这些紧急需求。所以确实有这个好处。 （17:48） 但我还想分享另一个心得，当我问自己“为什么我这么忙？”时，我意识到自己之所以这么忙，是因为我没有做出好的产品决策。现在你要理解，我已经有15年的产品开发经验了，做产品经理也有11年了。所以我觉得自己做得还不错。这是我的自我认知。但说实话，我并没有尽可能地做出好的产品决策。那么，我能举个例子说明一下吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Please.
turns.zh: 请讲。

turns.speaker: Shreyas Doshi
turns.en: So what I noticed is that you have a meeting about some product feature that somehow is requested or is really important, whatever the case might be. And so you have a meeting with some stakeholders and your engineering team, designers, et cetera. And then, you're trying to decide, "Should we build this or not?" And somebody says, "You know what? Why are we doing a meeting for this?" I read somewhere or I heard Bezos say that two-way doors, it's a two-way door. You quickly make a decision. Like, just quickly make a decision and move on. This is a two-way door. And so you say, "Yeah, that's right." And any time we hear something like that, two-way door, you're like, "Oh, that person's really smart, so I want to be like them." (19:32): So I noticed that myself and my team, we were making these kinds of decisions without very clearly thinking through customer motivation, very clearly thinking through differentiation, very clearly thinking through a distribution approach for whatever this feature is. And while it sounds like, "Oh, of course you should be doing this," I guarantee you this is not how most product teams work. They're talking about, "Well, is Bob the engineer going to be free? And when are they free? And if they are free, then let's build the feature." That's kind of how a lot of product decisions happen. (20:11): The challenge here with this kind of approach, and again, this is what happens in practice, I'm not talking about whatever theory you read, this is what happens in practice. So when you follow this approach and you assume that, "Oh, this is a two-way door, we can kill the feature," in reality, it doesn't work out that way, because here's what happens in reality. So in reality, you commit to the feature, and it's going to take five, six weeks to do it, and then a couple more weeks to make sure, to ramp it up, et cetera, right? And so now the feature is out, and now you have your Q1 QBR, right? Say two months from now you have your Q1 QBR, and you're going to present your business review, whatever. You're going to present what you did, "What did you do last quarter? How are your ships performing from last quarter?" (21:03): And so now, it's time to talk about this feature at the QBR, because you have to share that/ Now as you start talking about this feature, the CEO will ask, "So yeah, we launched the feature. I'm very glad we launched this feature. How is it doing?" And you want to be able to say, you are the PM leader, you want to be able to say something smart, and something that makes you look competent. But the challenge is the feature hasn't had much adoption. So I'm not going to ask anybody to raise hands, but I think most PMs are familiar with this conundrum. And of course, we are verbally very agile as product leaders. So what we say is we don't have data, so we use favorable anecdotes. (21:53): And so we say, "Yeah, we launched the feature, and you know what? This customer from this company really loves the feature." And we put in an anecdote, it's like, "Life-changing feature." It doesn't matter that they're the only person using it. That doesn't matter. "Life-changing feature," right? We use data when it favors us, we use anecdotes when it favors us. So anyway, so we present that. Now. we do have the sales counterpart in the room too, our sales counterpart, and they say, "You know what, though? We are still not winning many deals because of this feature." And so of course the CEO asks, "So what's up? Why aren't we winning deals, even though we have the feature?" (22:30): So the people on the customer side usually we respond, "Well, I'm glad we have the feature, but it's not full featured yet. We need all these other bells and whistles to meet the table stakes." So now, what happens? Somebody uttered the word, "Meet the table stakes." Now, it's over for you, because now, the only response you can give is, "Oh, yeah, that's already part of the plan." And now, you put your engineering leader on the spot and you say, "Alice, isn't it? Haven't we allocated engineers to it already?" And so now, Alice has to come up with some response, which is like, "Yeah, yeah, yeah, Carol and David are going to work on it. It's slotted for one of these sprints." (23:19): And so now, you exit the QBR, you high-five each other. Well, "Good job, team, great job," et cetera, et cetera. But now, you have signed up for even more work for a feature you should not have built in the first place. That's why we're busy. And through a product leader's life, what happens is we just accumulate all of this debt, feature after feature. So I guess what I'm saying, Lenny, is one of my other tactical tips would be sometimes it is useful to pause for two minutes, or two days, or two weeks before making that decision, right? Because frankly, most doors that look like two-way doors are actually one-way doors. They are two-way doors at Bezos' level, but as a PM leader, for you, they are a one-way door, and that's making you busy.

我的观察是，当你要讨论某个产品功能时，无论是用户需求还是产品本身的重要性如何，你都会召集相关利益方、工程团队、设计师等开会。然后大家开始讨论：“我们该不该开发这个功能？”这时有人会说：“哎呀，干嘛还要开会讨论这个？”我曾在某处读到或听贝索斯说过，所谓的“双向门”策略就是迅速做决策。就像他说的，“迅速做出决定，然后继续前进。这就是双向门。”所以你会附和道：“对啊，对啊。”但每次听到这种“双向门”的说法时，人们都会觉得对方很聪明，心想：“我也要学学他们。” （19:32）  

我发现自己和团队在做决策时，往往没有仔细思考客户需求、产品差异化或推广策略。虽然大家都说“当然应该做这个功能”，但现实中大多数产品团队的运作方式却截然不同。他们会问：“工程师鲍勃有空吗？什么时候有空？如果他有空，我们就开始开发这个功能。” 这才是大多数产品决策的真实场景。  

这种方法的挑战在于——这就是现实中的情况，不是理论上的——当你按照这种方法行事时，以为“这是个双向门，我们可以砍掉这个功能”，但现实并非如此。实际情况是，你先是承诺要开发这个功能，花五六周时间完成，再花几周时间测试、推广等。而当功能上线后，又要迎来季度业绩回顾（QBR），比如两个月后的QBR，你要汇报成果：“上季度做了什么？销售业绩如何？” （21:03）  

这时QBR上必须谈到这个功能，因为你得汇报进展。CEO会问：“功能上线了，很高兴我们推出了这个功能，表现如何？” 你想说点高明的话，让自己显得能干。但问题是这个功能用户接受度低。没人会举手发言，但大多数PM都遇到过这种困境。当然，我们作为产品负责人，口头上很灵活。于是我们说：“数据还不充分，先讲讲成功案例。” （21:53）  

我们会说：“功能上线了，有个客户特别喜欢。” 然后举例：“改变人生的功能。” 即便只有一个人在用也没关系，“改变人生的功能”，对吧？数据对我们有利时就用数据，对我们有利时就用案例。  

最后展示成果时，销售团队会说：“但因为这个功能我们还是拿不到很多单子。” CEO自然会问：“为什么？明明有功能了为什么还拿不到单子？” （22:30）  

客户那边的情况
通常我们会回应说：“嗯，我很高兴我们有这个功能，但它还不够完善。我们还需要其他各种附加功能才能达到基本要求。”那么接下来会怎样呢？有人抛出“达到基本要求”这个说法。这时你就陷入被动了，因为你唯一能做的回应就是：“哦，对啊，这本来就是计划的一部分啊。”接着你会当场质问工程负责人：“爱丽丝，是不是已经分配了工程师负责这项工作了？” 这时爱丽丝只能支支吾吾地回答：“是啊，是啊，卡罗尔和大卫会负责的，已经安排在某个冲刺周期里了。” （23:19）  
最后，大家在季度回顾会上互相击掌庆祝：“干得好，团队，太棒了！” 但实际上，你们又为一个本不该开发的功能承担了更多工作。这就是我们为何如此忙碌的原因。在产品负责人的职业生涯中，一个又一个功能的欠债只会越积越多。所以，莱尼，我想说的是，偶尔停下来两分钟、两天甚至两周再做决定，是很有必要的。因为说实话，大多数看似双向选择的门，实际上都是单向的。贝索斯那种级别的人或许能左右，但对产品经理来说，它们就是单向门——这正是导致我们忙得不可开交的原因。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I feel like you're a stand-up comedian/product manager. That was incredible. (24:28): This episode is brought to you by Vanta. When it comes to ensuring your company has top-notch security practices, things get complicated fast. Now, you can assess risk, secure the trust of your customers, and automate compliance for SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA, and more with a single platform, Vanta. Vanta's market-leading trust management platform helps you continuously monitor compliance, alongside reporting and tracking risk. Plus, you can save hours by completing security questionnaires with Vanta AI. (25:02): Join thousands of global companies that use Vanta to automate evidence collection, unify risk management, and streamline security reviews. Get $1,000 off Vanta when you go to vanta.com/lenny. That's vanta.com/lenny. (25:21): I know it's Spotify, I heard one of their core values is, "Talk is cheap," but it's the virtue version of that. It's like, they actually prefer to talk more, and I think that's exactly what you're saying. Basically, spend more time on these things that seemingly seem just small little ideas and experiments.
turns.zh: 哇。我感觉你既是脱口秀喜剧演员，又是产品经理。太不可思议了。（24:28）：本期节目由Vanta赞助。若想确保公司拥有一流的安全实践，事情很快就会变得复杂起来。现在，您可以通过单一平台Vanta，评估风险、赢得客户信任，并自动化符合SOC 2标准、ISO 27001认证、HIPAA法规等多项合规要求。Vanta市场领先的信任管理平台助您持续监控合规情况，同时进行风险报告与追踪。此外，借助Vanta的AI技术，您还能节省数小时的安全问卷填写时间。（25:02）：全球数千家企业正借助Vanta实现证据收集自动化、统一风险管理并简化安全审核流程。访问vanta.com/lenny，即可享受1000美元优惠。（25:21）：我知道这是Spotify，我听说他们的核心价值观之一是“空谈无益”，但这里体现的是积极向上的精神。他们实际上更倾向于多交流，我觉得这正是你所说的意思。关键是，要在这些看似微不足道的想法和实验上多花时间。

turns.speaker: Shreyas Doshi
turns.en: Yep, thinking is cheap, so you should do more thinking, not less.
turns.zh: 没错，思考成本很低，所以你应该多思考，而不是少思考。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Shreyas, what's your second question?
turns.zh: 太棒了。Shreyas，你的第二个问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Shreyas Doshi
turns.en: Yes. So my second question, I have to get the words right, do I actually have good taste? Do I actually have good taste is my second question. And for me, I asked this question after, again, all of these things... By the way, everything I say, I have been that guy, I've made that mistake. So that's why I just have to admit to myself that, yes, I have made these mistakes. And one of the mistakes I made, this was when I was at Google, and I was relatively new to product, about less than five years. And at Google, there's some parts of Google where you would be told as an early career PM that like, "We don't do strategy here. Strategy is for MBAs, okay? We are all about execution, okay?" (26:47): So I'm in this environment, I'm naïve, and I look around me and I'm like, "Google is the most successful company on the planet," at the time, and they are saying this, and I'm hearing this consistently, so it must be right. It must be right. And so I start saying it. I start saying, "Oh, yeah, execution is everything, and we don't do strategy around here." And I even remember there were not that many PMs, but there was a PM at Google who was kind of like the same level as me, but he just had much more wisdom than me. And he was trying to nudge me into... Like, I was managing a product. And he's like, "Shreyas, what is your strategy here?" And I was like, I told him the same thing. Like, "Oh, no, no, what are you talking strategy? We don't need strategy. We just need to get shit done." That was the thing. (27:42): And so I kept repeating that mantra until I got to Twitter. So this is Twitter right after their IPO. And I saw Twitter had an incredible asset, which is the product and the network effects. It had other incredible assets, including the brand. It had other assets that were great, including the talent. And yet, this company was struggling, the product was struggling. And even if it wasn't struggling, it was making a lot of money. But the point is it was not meeting its potential. So that's when I realized, and it wasn't like some sudden realization, it took me six to nine months of being at Twitter. This is circa 2014. That's when I realized that, "Oh, my gosh, Twitter's biggest problem is a product strategy problem. The reason they're struggling is they don't have a real product strategy." (28:38): Now, of course, attempts were made to create a product strategy, but it wasn't a real compelling, cohesive product strategy. So that's when I realized the folly of like, "Oh, wait a minute..." I was at Google six years. I spent most of those six years saying like, "Ah, strategy's useless. There's no point to strategy. Execution is where it's at. "I'm like, "No, actually, I was wrong." And that got further solidified as I went to Stripe, and I was kind of now growing earlier stage products and trying to make them highly, highly successful. I saw an even greater value and importance of having a clear strategy. And so that made me realize, basically... (29:29): You know, we talk about taste, we all talk about taste, and it's about the beautiful pixels, and the perfect product, and the whatever else, the Steve Jobs-esque passion, and all of that, whatever it is. And yes, taste is about that, but I think there is something that we as product leaders, and certainly I did, needed to recognize about taste as just a factor in pretty much everything we do, which is like, do we have good taste around the beliefs we choose to create within ourselves as product leaders? And then, those beliefs end up dictating everything we do, including how we manage, how we lead, how we make decisions. And so it's that taste I'm talking about when I say, "Do I really have good taste?" (30:28): And when I asked myself this question, and again, I really had to dig deep. It wasn't easy, but at some point I realized that no, actually, I don't have good taste. I don't have good taste in how I choose to evaluate things that come my way. Again, not in terms of the product, because by that time I had skills to say, "Well, this should not be a two-step flow. This should be a three-step flow," whatever the case may be. But I still did not have good taste in terms of how I choose what are the things I choose to believe, how do I learn, who do I learn from, what content I learned from, what content I resonate with? And then, I went on this journey to try to develop that better taste.
turns.zh:
是的。所以我的第二个问题是，我得确认自己的品味是否真的出色。「我是否真的有好的品味」就是我的第二个问题。对我而言，我提出这个问题，是因为经历了种种事情之后……顺便说一句，我所说的每一句话，我自己都曾犯过同样的错误。所以我必须承认，自己确实犯过这些错误。其中一个错误发生在谷歌时期，当时我刚入行产品管理不到五年。在谷歌，有些部门会告诉初级产品经理：“我们这里不搞战略，战略是MBA的事儿，懂吗？我们只专注于执行，懂吗？” （26:47）：在那样的环境中，我天真无知，环顾四周，谷歌可是全球最成功的公司啊，他们总这么说，而且我听得耳朵起茧，所以觉得肯定没错。肯定没错。于是我也开始附和：“哦，对啊，执行才是关键，我们这里不搞战略。” 我甚至记得当时谷歌没多少产品经理，但有个和我级别差不多的PM，他比我明智得多。他试图引导我：“Shreyas，你的产品战略是什么？” 我回答：“哦，不不不，谈什么战略？我们只需要把事儿做成。” 就是这样。（27:42）这种固执一直持续到我加入Twitter。当时Twitter刚上市不久。我发现Twitter有不可思议的资产——产品本身和网络效应，还有品牌等其他优势，甚至人才储备也相当出色。然而这家公司却举步维艰，产品陷入困境。即便不算举步维艰，至少他们赚得盆满钵满，但关键是未能发挥出全部潜力。直到2014年左右，我在Twitter待了六到九个月后，才意识到：「天哪，Twitter最大的问题在于产品战略缺失。产品战略的缺失才是他们深陷困境的根源。」（28:38）当然，Twitter也曾尝试制定产品战略，但始终缺乏真正引人注目、连贯一致的战略。就在那时，我意识到自己犯了致命错误——「哦，等等……」我在谷歌待了六年，大部分时间都在宣扬「战略无用，执行才是王道」。但后来去Stripe后，面对早期产品，我意识到清晰的战略价值非凡。这让我深刻领悟到，所谓「品味」，既关乎美观的像素、完美的产品设计，也关乎乔布斯式的激情，但归根结底，产品领导者需要认识到，品味贯穿于我们工作的方方面面——比如，作为产品领导者，我们选择构建的信念体系是否有良好的品味？而这些信念最终会主导我们的所有行动，包括管理方式在内。
我们的领导方式，我们的决策方式。所以当我问自己“我真的有好品味吗？”时，我所说的品味正是指这方面。（30:28）当我问自己这个问题时，又一次，我不得不深入反思。这并不容易，但最终我意识到，不，实际上我并没有好品味。具体来说，我在评估眼前事物时缺乏正确的判断力。当然，产品层面除外——那时我已经具备了专业判断能力，比如“这不应该是一个两步流程，而应该是一个三步流程”之类的。但在选择相信什么、如何学习、向谁学习、从何种内容中获取启发等方面，我仍然缺乏良好的判断力。于是，我踏上了培养这种更高品味的探索之旅。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I'm hearing is people focus maybe too much on the output, like the experience, these experience design taste versus what they choose to take in as informing their taste, and what they see as an example of great and correct. Is that what you're saying?
turns.zh: 我听到的是，大家可能过于关注输出的结果，比如体验设计的品味，以及人们用来判断品味的标准——他们认为什么是正确的范例，又把什么视为错误的范例。您是这个意思吗？

turns.speaker: Shreyas Doshi
turns.en: Yeah. And look, taste is about the ability to identify what is really good, without needing to see its results, because, look, it requires zero taste right now for anybody to say, "Oh, that CEO of NVIDIA is a genius, right? Jensen is a genius." If you are saying that in 2024, it actually requires zero taste, because you can just look up NVIDIA stock price. It requires zero skill. But to be able to say that in 2010, you have to realize Jensen Huang didn't change much between 2010 and 2024. So Lenny, even in sports, there's this saying, "Game recognize game," and that's about taste. (32:59): But what we need to understand is it's game recognize game before the game is called, right? Like, game recognize game in the practice session. Because it takes no genius right now to say, "Well, Patrick Mahomes is great quarterback," or, "Virat Kohli is a great cricketer," or whatever else. It requires no genius to do that. It requires zero taste. So I also believe some of us, especially as we get more senior, and we get more successful, and we just get a lot more scope, and responsibility, and a lot of accolades, we become these tough graders. Like, "I don't like anything," right? Like, "Ah, this is crap, this is crap, this is crap." Again, that requires zero taste. Anybody can say that. Anybody can just say, "Everything is horrible." (33:53): So I do think there is something about being able to understand that, and I think I'll share some examples. This two-way door thing, so let me just share a few observations, if I might. So the first one is we get overly excited about cool metaphors, okay? Like, one-way door, two-way doors. There's some guy, I don't know who it is, I just read somewhere, there's some guy who had written a blog post about this idea, but he called it reversible and irreversible decisions, and it was the same idea. And I think somebody was lamenting that that did not catch on, reversible and irreversible decisions. But what caught on is two-way door and one-way door. What's the difference? The only difference is you got attracted to the catchy metaphor, and the other one is the authority bias, because Bezos said it. (34:58): Take another example, we get very impressed with alliterations. I'm serious, we get very impressed with alliterations. Okay, so how many of us love fail fast? Fail fast, okay, nobody's going to raise hands now. Okay, fine. Maybe you truly don't love fail fast. How about fast follow? How many of you love fast follow? Let's consider that, like fail fast, "We're going to fail fast." What if that thing were called fail quickly? It's the same meaning. Do you think you would be as attracted to that idea if it were called fail quickly?
turns.zh: 是的。你看啊，品味其实是判断事物是否真的优秀的能力，无需看到结果就能做出判断。比如现在就说英伟达的首席执行官詹森·黄是天才，这不需要任何品味，因为你只要看看英伟达的股价就知道了。但如果你在 2024 年这么说，那确实不需要任何品味，因为你可以直接查阅英伟达的股价。这不需要任何技巧。但如果你在 2010 年这么说，你就得意识到詹森·黄在 2010 年到 2024 年间变化不大。所以，莱尼，甚至在体育领域也有句话叫“行家识行家”，这说的就是品味。（32:59）但我们需要明白的是，在比赛开始前就得能识别出行家，对吧？比如在训练场上就能识别出行家。因为现在说帕特里克·马霍姆斯是伟大的四分卫，或者维拉特·科利是出色的板球运动员，这不需要任何天赋。这不需要任何品味。所以我也认为，我们中有些人，尤其是随着职位晋升、事业成功、责任加重、荣誉增多之后，会变得成为严苛的评判者。比如“我什么都不喜欢”，或者“这太糟糕了，这太糟糕了，这太糟糕了”。但这又不需要任何品味。任何人都能这么说。（33:53）所以我确实认为理解这一点很重要，我想我会分享一些例子。比如双向门这个概念，让我分享几个观察点。如果可以的话。第一个是我们对酷炫的比喻过于兴奋了，对吧？比如单向门、双向门。有个家伙，我不知道是谁，我在某个地方读到过，他写了一篇关于这个概念的博客文章，但他称之为可逆和不可逆的决策，而意思是一样的。我觉得有人还在感叹可逆和不可逆的决策没有流行起来。但流行起来的却是双向门和单向门。有什么区别呢？唯一的区别就是你被吸引了这个吸引人的比喻，而另一个是权威偏差，因为贝索斯说了这句话。（34:58）再举个例子，我们对头韵词印象深刻。我是认真的，我们对头韵词印象深刻。好吧，有多少人喜欢“快速失败”？快速失败，对吧？现在没人举手了。好吧，也许你们真的不喜欢快速失败。那么“快速跟进”呢？有多少人喜欢快速跟进？让我们考虑一下，比如快速失败，“我们要快速失败”。如果这个叫快速失败呢？意思是一样的。你觉得如果叫快速失败，你会对这个想法有同样大的吸引力吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 不会。

turns.speaker: Shreyas Doshi
turns.en: Probably not, so what changed? The only thing that changed is one is an alliteration. So I see this in everything. Like, let's see, the other one is we also get very impressed with complicated charts and math we don't understand. And some of you product leaders who are at the top of the game, you actually use this as a strategy. So as I realized that here's the outcome of that, asking myself that question, was that what I realized is everybody says, "Oh, I'm a first principle thinker. I am a rigorous thinker," whatever. (36:41): But I realized that if I really want to be that, I have to shed a lot of these just patterns that were just built in me, and I kind of have to evaluate the idea separate from all of its social proof, and authority proof, and whatever else. And that ended up being a meaningful change in my growth as a product leader, because the moment I started shedding these kinds of social proofs, and authority proofs, and all of that, it just made me a much... We all again think we are critical thinkers, but we are not, right? So it made me a more critical thinker.
turns.zh: 可能不是吧，那有什么变化呢？唯一的变化就是“alliteration”这个词了。所以我到处都能看到这种现象。比如，举个例子，另一种情况是我们对复杂的图表和数学公式印象深刻，但其实自己根本看不懂。还有一些身处行业顶尖的Product Leader们，甚至把这当作一种策略。后来我意识到，问自己这个问题后，我得到的结论是，每个人都会说：“哦，我是个基于第一性原理思考的人。我是个严谨的思考者”，诸如此类。但我发现，如果真想做到这一点，就必须摒弃那些根深蒂固的思维模式，必须将想法与社会认同、权威证明等因素分开评估。这最终成了我作为Product Leader成长过程中的一次重大转变，因为当我开始摒弃这些社会认同、权威证明之类的因素时，整个人都变得更加……我们都自以为是批判性思考者，但其实并非如此，对吧？所以这让我成为了一个更具批判性思维的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to move on to the next question, just so we can get through some of these questions. Before I do, can you just show people your notes real quick, just like show it from a distance? This is how Shreyas plans for something like this. There's color coding, I wish I understood what was going on there.
turns.zh: 我想直接进入下一个问题，这样我们就能把这些问题都过一遍了。在开始之前，你能不能快速给观众展示一下你的笔记？就远距离展示一下？这就是Shreyas规划这类活动的方式。里面有颜色编码，我真希望能明白这里的逻辑。

turns.speaker: Shreyas Doshi
turns.en: People ask me, "What's your favorite note-taking app?" It's a common question I get, and I say this, right? It's a $5... Like I guess the pen costs $3, and I think the Office Depot clipboard costs-
turns.zh: 有人问我：“你最喜欢的笔记应用是什么？” 这是个常见问题，我通常会这么回答：5美元……比如笔可能3美元，Office Depot的剪贴板大概

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wait, doesn't that pen... Does it have the different color clicky thing?
turns.zh: 等等，那支笔……它有不同颜色的按压笔头吗？

turns.speaker: Shreyas Doshi
turns.en: Yes, yes, yeah. A [inaudible 00:38:04]. Yeah, exactly. This is great.
turns.zh: 对，对，嗯。（笑声）太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's going to be another podcast episode. Okay, so we want to try to do two more questions. We have six minutes left. The last one's a bonus, so maybe we touch on it briefly. Shreyas, what's your third question?
turns.zh: 这会成为另一期播客内容。好的，我们还想再回答两个问题。现在还剩六分钟。最后一个是加分题，或许可以简单提一下。Shreyas，你的第三个问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Shreyas Doshi
turns.en: So my third question is why does my job feel so frustrating? Why does my job feel so frustrating? And it goes back to the point that, look, I loved, loved my PM leadership job. I just absolutely loved it. And I think looking back, I would not have exchanged it for anything else, any other experience. That said, there were daily frustrations. There were daily frustrations in that job, and a lot of it has to do with the fact that the PM leader's job is extremely lonely. The PM's job, the PM's on your team, their job is also lonely. But a PM leader's job is further lonelier. So there's that. There's also what I learned at the time when I started asking this question is that our jobs get frustrating when we behave, most of the time, in misalignment with our superpowers and who we truly are at our core. (39:32): Okay, so for me, as I was evaluating that question, it's like, "Why am I getting frustrated every day? I love the job, I love the macro, but I do not like the micro. And so why is that?" And that's when I actually... There's a simple framework that I've shared, which is you can be doing your work at three levels. Product work happens at three levels. There's the impact level, there's the execution level, and there's the optics level. My epiphany as I was exploring this question was I have a preferred level at which I like to operate, but if most of the day, and most of the week, and most of the month, I am forcing myself to operate in not my happy place, in my non-default level, that makes me very frustrated. (40:33): So many product leaders, their happy place is the execution level. In my case, my happy place is the impact level. So that is fine. Your happy place can be whatever level, it doesn't matter. But the point is, as you go higher up in the corporate ladder, no matter what kind of company it is, you are now going to have to spend a lot of time on optics, at the optics level. And I have willpower, I have the skills to do it, I have all of that. So it's not about willpower or skills, but willpower is finite. So as I spent day in and day out, just mostly doing optics work, I realized I was not happy and I was getting frustrated. And so that's when I realized the solution, which is I have to abandon the traditional path, that like, "Oh, after this level, I'm supposed to do this, and then I'm supposed to do this, and then this is what society expects. This is what my mom expects. What will people say on LinkedIn when they see my LinkedIn profile?" Like, "Oh, he has this progression, this, and then what stopped? Why did it stop?" (41:49): So when I realized this, I said, when a team grew to a certain size, so when I was at Stripe and I realized this, when the team I was managing, it had a fan out of about 50 people, so this includes engineers and everything, I said, "This is enough." Because for me, any time a team goes to like 50s, and 100s, and beyond, it is a law of corporations that you're going to have to spend a lot of time at the optics level. So instead of just pushing, pushing through against who I truly am, what did I do? I just went back to more of an earlier stage product, and then I was fine with like, "You know what? I'm not going to just play the corporate game," as an example. (42:34): So I guess my suggestion would be identify your superpowers, and like Shakespeare said, "To thine own self be true." Just be honest to yourself. Operate your career and make your career decisions not out of expectation, not out of envy, like the LinkedIn envy of like, "Oh, this person is at a different level. We both went to the same grad school, so I got..." No, identify your superpowers, because if you identify your superpowers and work in accordance with them, you will do the best work of your life. You will love it, and you will be great at it, and you won't have that frustration.
turns.zh:
接下来我的第三个问题是，为什么我的工作让我感到如此沮丧？为什么我的工作让我感到如此沮丧？这要回到一个关键点：看，我曾深爱、深爱我的产品经理领导职位。我真的非常热爱它。回首往事，我绝不会用它去换取任何其他职位或经历。话虽如此，日常工作中还是有诸多令人沮丧之处。这份工作之所以令人沮丧，很大程度上是因为产品经理的职位极其孤独。产品经理在团队中的角色同样孤独，但产品经理的领导职位则更加孤立。所以这就是原因。还有一点，我在开始探究这个问题时发现，当我们的大部分工作与自身的核心优势和真实自我严重不符时，工作就会变得令人沮丧。（39:32）：好的，我在评估这个问题时发现：“为什么我每天都感到沮丧？我热爱这份工作，也热爱宏观层面，但不喜欢微观层面。这到底是为什么？”就在那时，我意识到……我分享过一个简单框架：你可以在三个层面开展工作。产品工作分为三个层级：影响层、执行层和展示层。探索这个问题的顿悟在于，我有一个自己喜欢的操作层级，但如果一天、一周、一个月的大部分时间，我都在强迫自己在非舒适区（非默认层级）工作，这会让我非常沮丧。（40:33）：许多产品经理的舒适区在执行层级。就我而言，我的舒适区在影响层级。这没关系。但关键是，当你在企业层级中晋升时，无论公司性质如何，你都必须花大量时间在展示层级上。我有意志力、有技能做到这些。但意志力是有限的。当我日复一日主要做展示层面的工作时，我意识到自己不快乐，也越来越沮丧。于是我意识到解决方案是放弃传统路径。比如，“达到这个级别后，就该做这个，再做那个，这是社会期望的，是我妈妈期望的。当人们在领英上看到我的个人资料时会怎么说？”诸如，“哦，他取得了这样的进步，然后为什么停下了？” （41:49）：当我意识到这一点时，我说。当团队规模达到一定规模时，比如我在Stripe时，我意识到，当我管理的团队达到约50人（包括工程师等所有成员）时，我说：“够了。”因为对我来说，当团队规模达到50人以上、100人以上时，企业法则就是你必须在展示层级上花费大量时间。所以与其违背真实自我强行前行，我做了什么？我回归到更早期的产品阶段。然后我就没事了。就像莎士比亚说的：“忠实于你自己。”诚实面对自己。规划职业生涯、做出职业决策时，不应出于期待，不应出于嫉妒，比如领英上的攀比心理：“哦，那个人达到了不同级别。我们都去过那里。”
同样是在研究生院，所以我得了…… 不，认清自己的超能力吧，因为如果你能认清自己的超能力并据此行动，你就能做出人生中最出色的工作。你会热爱这份工作，也会做得很出色，更不会感到沮丧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I wish we had an hour for every single one of these questions, I feel like there's so much more to get into. We have 40 seconds. Do you want to touch on your last question or do you want to leave that for a follow-up discussion?
turns.zh: 真希望我们能为每个问题都留出一个小时来探讨，我觉得还有太多内容可以深入挖掘。不过我们只有40秒时间。你是想现在回答最后一个问题，还是留到后续讨论？

turns.speaker: Shreyas Doshi
turns.en: Let's touch on it, let's touch on it.
turns.zh: 那就快速聊聊吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, we got to go though in 30 seconds.
turns.zh: 好的，我们得在30秒内结束了。

turns.speaker: Shreyas Doshi
turns.en: All right. My last question is am I really listening? Okay, and this is perhaps the hardest one for me, because I thought, of course I'm a good listener because I listen, then I recap, and I make eye contact, and I tell them, "This is what I heard," And all of that nonsense. I realized there is an entirely other level to listening, which once you understand that there's an entirely other level to listening, that is what enables you to be a world-class leader. And so that is what I guess my last takeaway is, is ask yourself, "Am I really listening?" If you want resources, there are very few people who actually talk about what that real listening means. I would refer you to what Rick Rubin says about listening, I would refer you to what [inaudible 00:44:30] said about listening, and what Drucker said about listening as some pointers.
turns.zh: 好的。我最后一个问题是，我真的在倾听吗？好吧，这对我来说可能是最难回答的，因为我总以为自己是个好听众——我会倾听、总结要点、保持眼神交流，还会说“我听到了这些”之类的。但后来我意识到，倾听还有更深的层次。一旦你理解了这个层次，它就能助你成为世界级的领导者。所以我想说的是，要问自己：“我真的在倾听吗？” 如果你想获取更多资源，真正探讨深度倾听含义的人并不多。我推荐你看看里克·鲁宾（Rick Rubin）关于倾听的见解，[未听清00:44:30]关于倾听的论述，以及德鲁克（Drucker）关于倾听的观点，作为参考。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Shreyas, you said you were going to hang out for the next hour somewhere. You want to share that real quick, and then we'll get off?
turns.zh: 太棒了。施雷亚斯（Shreyas），你说你接下来要在某个地方待一个小时。你能快速分享一下行程安排吗？然后我们就结束了。

turns.speaker: Shreyas Doshi
turns.en: Yes, I will maybe try to hang out in the back part of the room.
